blocks.heading: Money with conditions
text: Teodora runs a two-person record label in Belgrade. On 4 May 2026 she agrees to pay Ines, a mastering engineer in Berlin, 0.012 BTC for six tracks.
They have worked together twice. Neither wants to be the one who says "and what if you don't".

blocks.heading: Pay first or deliver first
text: Pay up front and Teodora is trusting Ines. Deliver first and Ines is trusting Teodora. There is no third option between two strangers on a wire.
Unless the money can be sent somewhere neither of them controls.

blocks.heading: An output is not "owned"
text: Every output carries a small program that says what unlocking it requires. The ordinary one asks for a signature matching a hash - that is all an address is.

blocks.label: the script behind a normal address

blocks.heading: So ask for something else
text: Nothing privileges "one signature". The language can ask for two out of three.

blocks.heading: Dragan is not a company
text: He is a mutual friend who mixes live sound, is not paid for this, and will never touch the money on his own - two keys are needed, and he only has one.
His entire power is to break a tie by siding with whoever he thinks is right.

blocks.heading: And a way out if everyone vanishes

blocks.alt: A locked output with two spending paths: any two of three signatures, or a refund to Teodora after thirty days
blocks.caption: `OP_CHECKSEQUENCEVERIFY` puts the deadline in the output itself, where nobody can decline to honour it.

blocks.question: A transaction already has an `nLockTime` field meaning "not valid before then". Why did bitcoin need a whole new opcode for timelocks?
answer: Because `nLockTime` is set by the person spending, and they can simply not set it. It constrains a transaction you are already writing - it cannot constrain a future spender.
BIP-65 and BIP-112 moved the condition into the **output**, so it binds whoever comes to unlock it. The receiver of the coin inherits the rule instead of choosing it.

blocks.heading: The bug she has to work around
text: `OP_CHECKMULTISIG` pops one item more off the stack than it needs - a mistake in the 2009 implementation.
It cannot be fixed, because changing it would split the network. Every multisig spend to this day pushes a dummy `OP_0` for the operator to throw away.
Worth sitting with. A consensus rule is not code you maintain - it is code every participant must agree to change simultaneously.
So an obvious one-line bug becomes a permanent feature of the format, and everything built afterwards accommodates it.

blocks.heading: Teodora only sends to an address
text: She does not put that whole script in the transaction. She pays to a **hash** of it, and whoever spends must reveal the script and satisfy it.
Pay-to-script-hash, BIP-16: her label's bank transfer screen sees a normal-length address, and the complexity is entirely on the spending side.

blocks.heading: What Script deliberately cannot do
text: There are no loops. No recursion, no jumps backwards, no unbounded anything.
The cost of running a script is known from its length before it runs, which is why no bitcoin transaction can ever make a node spin forever.

blocks.heading: And what it cannot do by accident

text: The script checks signatures and elapsed blocks. It has no idea whether the master was delivered, whether it was any good, or whether Ines answered her email.
Every dispute worth having is outside what the machine can see. That is precisely why the third key belongs to a person - and it is the hole chapter 5 ends on.

blocks.heading: One sentence worth keeping
text: A condition on money can only ever be about things the chain can observe, which is signatures and time, and nothing else whatsoever.
Ethereum looked at that constraint and removed it. Next: what the other model buys, and what it costs.
